title: Anatomy of Flowering Plants
tagline: Meristems, tissue systems, internal structure of roots, stems and leaves, and secondary growth in dicot stems and roots.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Biology registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Morphology describes the outside of a plant; anatomy describes the inside. In this chapter we study how flowering plants are built at the tissue level, starting with meristems, the regions of active cell division. We then look at the permanent tissues and the three tissue systems, and we examine the internal structure of roots, stems and leaves. Finally, we study secondary growth, the increase in girth that makes stems and roots thicker in many dicots.

facts.label: Syllabus unit
facts.value: Structural Organisation in Animals and Plants

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Meristems; simple and complex tissues; tissue systems; root, stem and leaf anatomy; secondary growth in dicot stems and roots

learningOutcomes: Classify meristems by location and origin.
Describe simple and complex tissues and their functions.
Identify the epidermal, ground and vascular tissue systems.
Compare the internal structure of dicot and monocot roots, stems and leaves.
Explain secondary growth in dicot stems and roots.

blocks.text: Meristems are regions of actively dividing cells. They are the source of new cells in a plant. Meristems are classified by location and by origin. The apical meristems at the tips of roots and shoots are responsible for length growth. The lateral meristems are responsible for increase in girth. There are also intercalary meristems in some plants. Understanding where a meristem is located helps explain the kind of growth it produces.

items: Meristems are regions of active cell division.
Apical meristems are at the tips of roots and shoots.
Lateral meristems increase girth.
Intercalary meristems occur between mature tissues in some plants.
Location helps explain function.

items.text: The root tip has an apical meristem, which adds new cells at the front of the root as it grows into the soil.
items.note: The meristem is the engine of growth, but the cells it produces later specialise into different tissues.

blocks.text: Plant tissues are organised into three tissue systems: the epidermal, ground and vascular systems. The epidermal system forms the outer covering and often helps protect the plant and control water loss. The ground system includes tissues such as parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma, which perform functions like storage, support and photosynthesis. The vascular system includes xylem and phloem, which conduct water, minerals and food. A good way to work is to identify the system first, then the tissues within it.

items: The three tissue systems are epidermal, ground and vascular.
Epidermal tissue forms the outer layer.
Ground tissue includes parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
Vascular tissue includes xylem and phloem.

items.text: The vascular bundle is part of the vascular system and contains both xylem and phloem. In a section, its position helps distinguish roots from stems.
items.note: Identification is easier when you think in systems first and individual tissues second.

learn.title: Internal structure of root and stem

blocks.text: A transverse section of a dicot root shows an outer epidermis, cortex and a central vascular region with xylem and phloem. In a dicot stem, the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring, with cambium between them in many cases. A monocot stem usually has scattered vascular bundles. These differences in arrangement are useful for identifying a section as root or stem and as monocot or dicot.

items: Dicot roots have a central vascular cylinder.
Dicot stems often have vascular bundles in a ring.
Monocot stems usually have scattered vascular bundles.
The arrangement of bundles helps identification.

items.text: In a dicot stem, the vascular bundles in a ring leave a central pith region, while in a monocot stem, the bundles are scattered and a distinct central pith is not formed in the same way.
items.note: The pattern matters more than the thickness of any one layer when identifying a section.

blocks.text: A leaf is adapted to photosynthesis and gas exchange. Its internal structure includes an epidermis, often with stomata for gas exchange, and a mesophyll inside, which in dicots is often differentiated into palisade and spongy tissues. The vascular bundles in a leaf are arranged as veins. The difference between dicot and monocot leaves can be seen in the venation and in the arrangement of mesophyll and bundle sheath cells.

items: A leaf has an epidermis and a mesophyll.
Stomata allow gas exchange.
Dicot leaves often have palisade and spongy mesophyll.
Venation and mesophyll arrangement differ between dicots and monocots.

items.text: In a dicot leaf, the palisade mesophyll is usually on the upper side and the spongy mesophyll below, with air spaces that help gas exchange.
items.note: The structure is related to function; the separation of palisade and spongy tissue is not just a label.

blocks.text: Secondary growth is the increase in thickness that occurs in many dicot stems and roots. It is brought about by the vascular cambium and the cork cambium. The vascular cambium adds secondary xylem inwards and secondary phloem outwards, and the cork cambium produces the protective outer layers. Over time, this produces annual rings in the wood, and it leads to the distinction between heartwood and sapwood. Bark is the tissue outside the vascular cambium.

items: Secondary growth increases girth in many dicots.
Vascular cambium produces secondary xylem and phloem.
Cork cambium produces outer protective tissue.
Annual rings form in many woody stems.
Heartwood and sapwood are two regions of older wood.

items.text: In a tree trunk, the inner part may become heartwood, which is older and often more durable, while the outer part remains sapwood, which is still active in conduction.
items.note: Secondary growth is not the same as the lengthening of a stem; it happens later and increases thickness.

keyPoints: Meristems are regions of active cell division.
Apical meristems add length; lateral meristems add girth.
The three tissue systems are epidermal, ground and vascular.
Xylem conducts water and phloem conducts food.
Dicot and monocot stems differ in vascular bundle arrangement.
Secondary growth is caused by vascular cambium and cork cambium.
Annual rings and heartwood/sapwood are features of secondary growth.
examFocus: When identifying a section, first decide whether it is root or stem, and then monocot or dicot, using bundle arrangement and other structural features.
Do not confuse xylem and phloem positions by memorising one diagram only; look at where the tissues are in the section.

vocabulary.meaning: A region of actively dividing plant cells.
A differentiated tissue made of cells that no longer divide actively.
A simple tissue with thin-walled living cells, often used for storage and photosynthesis.
The vascular tissue that conducts water and minerals.
The vascular tissue that conducts organic nutrients.
Increase in thickness due to activity of lateral meristems.

questions.prompt: Which tissue conducts water and minerals in a plant?
questions.commonMistake: Choosing phloem, which conducts food, not water.

questions.prompt: Secondary growth in dicots is mainly due to the activity of:
questions.explanation: Secondary growth is brought about by lateral meristems such as vascular cambium and cork cambium.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing apical meristem, which adds length, not thickness.

questions.prompt: Distinguish xylem from phloem by function.
questions.answer: Xylem conducts water and minerals from roots to other parts; phloem conducts organic food materials from sources to sinks.
questions.explanation: The key functional difference is what each tissue conducts.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the tissues by appearance alone without stating function.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the vascular bundle arrangement in a typical dicot stem and a monocot stem?
questions.answer: In a typical dicot stem, vascular bundles are arranged in a ring; in a monocot stem, they are usually scattered.
questions.explanation: The arrangement of bundles is one of the main differences between dicot and monocot stems.
questions.commonMistake: Saying both have the same arrangement, or depending on thickness alone.

questions.prompt: Explain the role of vascular cambium in secondary growth.
questions.answer: Vascular cambium is a lateral meristem that adds secondary xylem towards the inside and secondary phloem towards the outside. This increases the thickness of the stem or root, and over time it produces wood and contributes to annual rings.
questions.explanation: Secondary growth is about making the inside of the stem or root thicker, and vascular cambium is the main tissue responsible for that.
questions.commonMistake: Saying secondary growth increases length, or forgetting that both secondary xylem and secondary phloem are produced.
